title: Hierarchical Copper with Inherent Hydrophobicity Mitigates Electrode Flooding for High-Rate CO2 Electroreduction to Multicarbon Products
abstract: Copper is currently the material with the most promise as catalyst to drive carbon dioxide (CO2) electroreduction to produce value-added multicarbon (C2+) compounds. However, a copper catalyst on a carbon-based gas diffusion layer electrode often has poor stabilityespecially when performing at high current densitiesowing to electrolyte flooding caused by the hydrophobicity decrease of the gas diffusion layer during operation. Here, we report a bioinspired copper catalyst on a gas diffusion layer that mimics the unique hierarchical structuring of Setaria’s hydrophobic leaves. This hierarchical copper structure endows the CO2 reduction electrode with sufficient hydrophobicity to build a robust gas−liquid−solid triple-phase boundary, which can not only trap more CO2 close to the active copper surface but also effectively resist electrolyte flooding even under high-rate operation. We consequently achieved a high C2+ production rate of 255 ± 5.7 mA cm −2 with a 64 ± 1.4% faradaic efficiency, as well as outstanding operational stability at 300 mA cm−2 over 45 h in a flow reactor, largely outperforming its wettable copper counterparts.

■ INTRODUCTION Electrochemical upgrading of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide (CO2) into valuable carbon-based fuels and feedstocks, ideally driven by electricity from renewable sources, offers an attractive pathway to reduce waste gas emissions, leading to a closed loop for carbon footprint.1−3 Currently, copper (Cu) is perhaps the most paradigmatic catalyst capable of coupling C− C bonds, yielding deeply reduced products such as ethylene,4 ethanol,5 acetate,6 and n-propanol.7 The CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) on Cu-based catalysts has reached much increased faradaic efficiencies (FEs) and selectivity toward energy-dense C2+ products via strategies such as morphological control,8,9 introduction of dopants,10,11 and regulation of oxidation states.12,13 Nevertheless, the poor solubility of CO2 in water (∼35 mM at 298 K and 1 atm pressure)14 and the competing hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) considerably limit the C2+ partial current densities from being practical. For example, in a conventional H-shaped electrolyzer, the typical Cu catalyst9 known today can produce C2+ fuels with an FE of 60% at a current density of a mere 40 mA cm−2, which stands far below the industrially relevant requirement (>200 mA cm−2).15
In recent years, flow-cell CO2RR electrolyzers 4,8,16 have been engineered to circumvent the mass transport limitation, in which the gas reactants diffuse directly to the electrode− electrolyte interfaces, forming a gas−liquid−solid triple-phase
boundary where the CO2RR occurs. Moreover, highly alkaline electrolytes can be adopted to improve charge transfer kinetics and suppress the competing HER, which give rise to marked improvements in FE, selectivity, and reaction rate toward C2+ products.4,16 Although important advances have been made, recent studies4,8,17−19 have demonstrated that the stability of catalysts on the hydrophobic gas-diffusion layers (GDLs) was poor in flow reactors. One major reason for the instability is due to the electrolyte flooding caused by the reduced hydrophobicity of a GDL during the CO2RR process.
20,21 If GDL flooding occurs, CO2 diffusion toward the catalyst layer is blocked and high CO2RR rates can no longer be obtained. Various strategies have been employed to increase the hydrophobicity of GDL electrodes, such as binding with hydrophobic polymers or waxy alkanethiols.22,23 However, chemical modifications often have limitations: they can damage the intrinsic properties of catalytic electrodes, for example, the electrical conductivity.24 Janaḱy’s group25 has

demonstrated a zero gap electrolyzer cell that mitigates electrolyte flooding during CO2 electrolysis. However, the carbonate formation at the cathode becomes a major issue. Thus far, achieving more commercially relevant current densities, while preventing the flooding issue encountered at severe electrolysis, has remained a big challenge. In Nature, many plants such as Setaria have hydrophobic
leaves that allow water droplets to run off readily after morning dew or rain. The leaf of the Setaria looks macroscopically rough with a contact angle (CA) of 152.6° (Figure 1a and inset), which is within the regime of superhydrophobicity. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM; Figure 1b) uncovered many oriented needles on the Setaria’s leaves, which form unique micro/nanostructures. Consequently, available air can be trapped near the sharp microstructures to create an air cushion at the leaf−water interface (Figure 1c), leading to the striking hydrophobicity. By contrast, the smooth banana leaf contains rich wrinkles on the flat surface with a CA of a mere 55° (Figure S1), demonstrating its wetting nature. Inspired by Setaria’s leaves, we considered that a GDL
electrode with appropriate sharp architectures may prevent it from being wetted (Figure 1b). We thus engineered the GDL by growing hierarchically structured Cu dendrites consisting of sharp needles via a simple electrodeposition method. Using the resultant electrode, we achieve a C2+ production rate of 255 ± 5.7 mA cm−2 with an FE up to 64 ± 1.4%, far exceeding the performance of its wettable counterparts. The electrode also shows notable stability at 300 mA cm−2 after 45 h of
continuous operation. We attribute these results to the hydrophobic Cu hierarchical structure, which not only enables more CO2 trapped at the electrode−electrolyte interface, which increases the CO2RR rate and selectivity, but also offers a robust triple-phase interface that mitigates GDL flooding (Figure 1d).
■ RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Preparation and Characterizations of the Hierarchical Cu Electrode. Metallic materials commonly possess hydrophilic surfaces because of the high surface free energy.26,27 A popular approach to increase hydrophobicity of metals is to coat a hydrophobic polymer layer, which, unfortunately, often leads to reduced electrical conductivity.24,28 Very recently, Khan et al.29 created hierarchical micro−nano pyramidal textures on silicon, which allows the CO2 gas to be efficiently captured within the Si textures. Then, they placed the obtained CO2 plastron close to the smooth Cu wire catalyst for CO2RR study in an H-cell reactor. In another study, Wakerley et al.24 reported a bioinspired hydrophobicity on Cu dendrites by uniform 1-octadecanethiol coating, which enables a 74% selectivity for C2+ production in an H-cell reactor. However, this electrode allows only for current densities of <30 mA cm−2 to be reached owing to the reduced conductivity caused by 1-octadecanethiol modification. Moreover, its long-term stability at current densities relevant to commercial operation is questionable. Hence, their results, although fundamentally interesting, did not provide a clear
https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c01190 J. Am. Chem. Soc. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
B
prospect on the potential of alkanethiol-modified Cu dendrites for CO2 electrolysis at high current densities. We thus turned to synthesize a Cu catalyst with a high surface roughness via forming hierarchically sharp structures to increase hydrophobicity.26 Inspired by the needle-shaped microstructure on Setaria’s leaves, we prepared sharp Cu needles that assemble into hierarchical architectures. Generally, a hydrophobic surface has a positive Laplace pressure (Pz) from gas existing in a nano/microscale texture,30,31 which is determined by the following equation:
γ π φ α θ π φ= Ω − −i k jjj y { zzzP f sin cos sin 2z 0 (1)
where γ is the surface tension of the liquid, Ω is the density of the needle, f is the adhesion fraction of the liquid−solid interface, φ is the apex half-angle, θ0 is the static contact angle, and α is the tilt angle of the needle (Figure 2a and Figure S2). When the apex half-angle is 0° < φ < 20° and the tilt angle is −90° < α < +90°, Pz always has a positive value (Figure 2b and Figure S3). The analysis of this formula suggests that the
maximum Pz value can be achieved at φ = 7° and α = 0° (Figure 2b and Figure S3), revealing the marked hydrophobicity of the sharp structure. On the basis of the above considerations, we employed
electrodeposition as a scalable and simple method to prepare a desired hierarchical Cu catalyst composed of sharp needles on a GDL (see Experimental Section; Figure S4). For comparison, we also synthesized Cu particles by a hydrothermal route and deposited them on a GDL (see Experimental Section). The Xray diffraction (XRD) studies confirm the obtained structures to be metallic Cu (Figure 2c), whereas a slight surface oxidation was detected by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS; Figure S5) and Cu L-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS; Figure S6) measurements. After electrodeposition, the electrode was inspected under an optical microscope, which shows uniform coverage of Cu dendrites on the GDL (Figure 2d). The contact angle test gives a high CA value of 154° (inset in Figure 2d), revealing the hydrophobicity of the electrode where gas is expected to be trapped on the micro/ nanoscale. To verify that the observed hydrophobicity arises
https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c01190 J. Am. Chem. Soc. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
C
from the hierarchical architectures, we studied the structuring of the Cu catalyst by SEM. Figure 2e shows a representative SEM image of the as-prepared Cu catalyst electrodeposited at −0.7 V versus the Ag/AgCl reference electrode for 700 s. The SEM image exhibits highly hierarchical dendrites constructed by numerous sharp Cu needles (Figure S7). Close-up analysis of these needles reveals an average φ value of 11° (Figure 2f and Figure S8), which indicates a large Pz and thus outstanding hydrophobicity. Control experiments exhibit that the hydrophobicity increases gradually as the electrodeposition time increases, owing to the more hierarchically sharp structures of the resultant electrodes (Figure S9). A high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) image taken at the needle tip uncovers a well-resolved lattice spacing of 0.21 nm, corresponding to the (111) planes of cubic Cu (inset in Figure 2f). By contrast, uniform Cu particles deposited on the GDL also expose (111) planes, which possess a wettable surface with a CA value of 79° (Figure 2g−i and Figure S10). Our electrochemical roughness factor measurements yield values of 20.6 and 13.4 for Cu dendrites and particles, respectively (Figure S11). Thus, we have achieved remarkable hydrophobicity in the naked Cu catalyst on a GDL without surface modifications via suitable control of the structural hierarchy. We now study the surface behavior of the achieved
electrodes in CO2-saturated electrolytes. Considering that a single CO2 bubble reacts rapidly in 1 M KOH (Figure S12), we used 1 M KHCO3 as a replacement for investigations, which does not affect the surface chemistry of Cu electrodes. The hierarchical Cu electrode visibly traps CO2 molecules at the electrolyte−electrode interface, leading to a shiny surface (Figure 3a), analogous to the air trapping observed on a Setaria’s leaf (Figure 1c). Such a layer of gas thus enables the
formation of a gas−liquid−solid triple-phase boundary that permits improved CO2 mass transfer. However, the electrode composed of Cu particles displays underwater hydrophilicity (Figure S13), which could cause poor CO2 transfer as well as electrolyte flooding. We designed a homemade platform that enables the real-
time monitoring of hydrophobicity on the electrode surface under electrochemical conditions (Figure S14). The hydrophobic surface permits a well-defined aqueous KHCO3 droplet on the top of the hierarchical Cu electrode (Figure 3b). Applying a potential drives the oxygen evolution from the droplet (Figure 3c). We found that the hydrophobicity does not change appreciably after 10 min of electrochemical operation. The subtle decrease in droplet size is likely a result of oxygen formation that consumes water in the droplet (Figure 3c). Because superhydrophobic surfaces in air are often superaerophilic under water,32−34 we surmise the high aerophilicity of our designed hierarchical electrode. The CO2 adhesion experiments show that the CO2 bubble can immediately diffuse into the hierarchical Cu electrode once reaching the electrode surface (Figure 3d), confirming the superaerophilic feature.32,34 This result means that CO2 molecules can quickly transfer and accumulate at the active Cu surfaces in the electrolyte. By contrast, the CO2 bubble exhibits a “pinning state”32,35 on the Cu particles, which is retained on the electrode even up to 30 s (Figure 3e), indicating that CO2 transfer across this surface is limited.
CO2 Electroreduction in a Flow Cell. To experimentally probe the impact of the hierarchical Cu structure on CO2RR performance, we assessed the CO2 reduction activity of Cu dendrites and particles in a flow-cell reactor with 1 M KOH (see Experimental Section). We fed the cathode with CO2 gas at a flow rate of 24 mL min−1, and the outlet gas flow rate for
https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c01190 J. Am. Chem. Soc. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
D
each measurement was carefully tracked for gas product analysis (Figure S15). The linear sweep voltammetry curves in Figure 4a reveal that Cu dendrites give a more prominent reduction peak versus Cu particles, hinting at a faster CO2RR kinetics on Cu dendrites. Considering that charge transfer resistance (Rct) correlates with the electrons transferred from the catalyst surface to the reactants, we conducted electrochemical impedance spectroscopy. At the applied potential of −0.6 V versus RHE (reversible hydrogen electrode), our measurements yield small Rct values of merely 5.5 and 5.8 ohms for Cu dendrites and particles (Figure S16), respectively. CO2RR electrolysis (Figures S17−S19) displays that the hierarchical Cu dendrites can generate C2+ products at a range of applied potentials between −0.53 and −0.68 V versus RHE (Figure S20a). Figure 4b shows the evolution of C2+ products with a 30.1% FE at −0.53 V versus RHE on Cu dendrites. This FE rapidly increases to 64% at a more negative potential of −0.68 V versus RHE, corresponding to 30% ethylene, 8.5% acetate, 23.7% ethanol, and 1.6% n-propanol (Figure 4b, Figure S20a, and Table S1). The FE of C1 products drops from 25.2% to 4.2% when a negative potential from −0.53 to −0.68 V versus RHE was applied (Figure 4b and Figure S20a),
suggesting the promoted C−C coupling for the formation of C2+ products. At −0.68 V versus RHE, however, the Cu particles give a small C2+ FE of only 25.3% (Figure 4b, Figure S20b, and Table S2), which reasonably agrees with results on Cu particulate catalysts reported previously (Table S3). We spotlight that the C2+:C1 selectivity on Cu dendrites overwhelmingly outperforms Cu particles at all potentials examined (Figure S21). Remarkably, we obtained a maximum C2+:C1 selectivity of 15.4 on Cu dendrites at −0.68 V versus RHE, which is 19.3-fold higher than on Cu particles. Our measured geometric current densities for C2+ and C1 production on the two studied electrodes at various applied potentials are plotted in Figure 4c. Intriguingly, the Cu dendrites exhibits a maximum C2+ partial current density of 255 mA cm−2 at −0.68 V versus RHE. This result indicates that the hierarchical Cu electrode holds promise to operate at industrial electrolyzer-relevant current densities. By contrast, the Cu particles only offer a C2+ partial current density of 111 mA cm−2, even applying a more negative potential of −0.75 V versus RHE (Figure 4c). Further, the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA)-normalized current densities of Cu dendrites largely exceed that of Cu particles at various applied
https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c01190 J. Am. Chem. Soc. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
E
potentials (Figure S22), indicating its superior intrinsic CO2RR activity. Tafel studies yield a similar slope for ethylene (119 mV dec−1) and ethanol (111 mV dec−1) on the hierarchical Cu electrode (Figure 4d), suggesting that the two products share the same rate-determining step. The measured slopes for ethylene and ethanol production agree reasonably with previous reports,4,7 which are close to 118 mV dec−1 and suggest a rate-determining 1e− transfer involved in C−C bond formation between adsorbed *CO intermediates7,36,37 (Figure S23). By contrast, much higher Tafel slopes of 341 and 324 mV dec−1 for ethylene and ethanol were obtained on a Cu particulate electrode (Figure 4d), respectively, which imply that the processes were not determined by 1e− transfer. Motivated by the high C2+ FE (64%) and production rate (255 mA cm−2) achieved on the hierarchical Cu electrode, we turn to obtain the half-cell (cathodic) power conversion efficiency (PCE; see Experimental Section).38 The results (Figure 4e) show that the Cu dendrites can deliver a cathodic PCE for conversion to C2+ products of 41.2% at a total current density of 250 mA cm−2, far exceeding that of 16.5% observed on Cu particles. We also compared our CO2RR performance with those previously reported in terms of C2+ FE and C2+ partial current density. The results obtained on our hierarchical Cu structure represent the best performance reported to date as compared to other Cu dendrites documented in the literature12,24,39−43
for CO2RR catalysis (Figure 4f and Table S4). Aside from the alkaline electrolyte, our hierarchical Cu electrode also yields notable C2+ products in 1 M KHCO3 electrolyte with a C2+ FE of 52.2% and partial current density of 209 mA cm−2 at −0.78 V versus RHE (Figure S24). Furthermore, our control experiments using N2 gas feed instead of CO2 uncover that no carbon-based products could be detected (Figure S25), which excludes the possibility of KHCO3 as a reactant.
The operating stability of the CO2RR catalysts remains a challenge to their application, partially owing to the flooding issue described above. To assess the long-term stability of the hierarchical Cu electrode, we first run continuous CO2 electrolysis under a constant current density of 300 mA cm−2 for 10 h. The ratio of carbon-based products/(bi)carbonate during this process was consistently maintained at ∼20% (Figure S26). The electrode was found to be very stable under the harsh conditions, with only a slight increase in overpotential and small loss in C2+ selectivity in this time interval (Figure 4g and Table S5). Our measurements show that the initial pH of 13.64 in 1 M KOH electrolyte slightly reduces to 12.84 after 10 h of electrolysis, resulting in a ∼1 ohm increase in solution resistance (Figure S27). Through replacing the electrolyte occasionally, the overpotentials and FE could be maintained over a 45-h-long electrolysis at 300 mA cm−2 (Figure 4g). By stark contrast, the Cu particle electrode requires progressively increased overpotentials at this operating current and H2 dominates the products rapidly (Figure 4g and Table S6). At a smaller current density of 120 mA cm−2, the electrode can retain a C2H4 FE of ∼40% over 140 h of CO2 electrolysis (Figure S28). We attribute the remarkable performance stability to the robust hydrophobicity of the hierarchical Cu electrode that prevents flooding. Indeed, the GDL electrode after a long-term stability test was almost not flooded, in which no obvious carbonate crystallization can be observed (Figure S29). Post-mortem characterizations uncover that the dendritic morphology and metallic Cu phase (few Cu2O originate from surface oxidation) are well maintained (Figures S30−S32). The capillary pressure effect on the electrode structure is negligible (Figure S33). Importantly, we find that the surface hydrophobic and aerophilic features remain unchanged for the used electrode (Figures S34 and S35). No appreciable change in the ECSA was observed on our Cu dendrite electrode after different numbers of hours of CO2 electrolysis (Figure S36). These
https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c01190 J. Am. Chem. Soc. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
F
results together confirm the structural robustness of the new CO2RR cathode even working at high current densities, comparing favorably with various GDL electrodes reported previously (Table S7). To further verify the importance of the hydrophobicity on
the observed CO2RR performances, we intentionally destroyed the hydrophobicity of the hierarchical Cu electrode by air plasma bombardment and compared the resultant sample with the untreated one. Results show that the hierarchical morphology of the Cu catalyst is well retained after bombarding for 5 min, whereas its surface turns highly hydrophilic with a small water CA of 11° (Figure S37). Holding at 200 mA cm−2, we obtained a low C2+ FE of 39% on the hydrophilic Cu electrode, accompanied with improved H2 evolution (Figure S38). Moreover, long-term continuous CO2 electrolysis at 300 mA cm−2 revealed a quick decay of C2+ selectivity (Figure S39). The drop in C2+ selectivity could originate from the easy flooding of the treated electrode that hampers CO2 diffusion toward the catalyst. Finite-Element-Method Simulations and Operando Raman Spectroscopy. Next, we turn to combine the simulations and operando Raman spectroscopy to uncover the underlying reasons for the exceptional C2+ selectivity observed on our hierarchical Cu dendrite electrode. Recent studies have shown, both experimentally and computationally, that the alkali-metal-cation effect at the gas−liquid−solid interface can not only create a dipole field that stabilizes intermediates with large dipole moments (e.g., *CO2, *CO, and *OCCO) but also greatly reduce the *CO dimerization barrier, promoting C−C coupling.9,44,45 We thus applied finiteelement-method simulations46−48 to probe if the hierarchical Cu electrode could concentrate the electric field and cation concentration (see Experimental Section for details). We created dendrites composed of multiple needles to represent the Cu electrode immersed in an electrolyte. Our series of simulated results reveal that Cu dendrites with more needles and a smaller radius of curvature (ROC) exhibit a more enhanced local electrostatic field (Figures S40−S43). By contrast, Cu particles show an inferior local electrostatic field owing to the large ROC. Considering these factors, we thus constructed a model that closely resembles the experimentally observed structure (Figure 5a). Using the Gouy−Chapman− Stern method, we can assess the impact of electric field on the adsorbed K+ concentration, because this model permits the mapping of surface K+ density in the Helmholtz layer of the electrical double layer near the catalyst surface.46 Intriguingly, we observed a 10.5-fold increase in surface-adsorbed K+ concentration at the dendritic electrode (Figure 5a) as compared to the particulate counterpart (Figure 5b). These results therefore indicate highly concentrated K+ cations on the surface of the hierarchical Cu electrode, which could promote the formation of C−C bonds. To monitor the adsorbed CO2 reduction intermediates, we performed operando Raman spectroscopy in CO2-flowed 1 M KOH electrolyte at various applied current densities (Figure S44). We specifically chose the excitation wavelength to be 785 nm because it can yield large Raman intensity of related vibration modes.5,49 With increasing current density, two clear Raman peaks arise from the hierarchical Cu electrode (Figure 5c), where the peak at ∼2070 cm−1 corresponds to the stretching vibration mode of absorbed CO* at the top site.5,49,50 According to Masuda and Hwang’s previous work,51,52 the additional peak at lower energy (∼1980 cm−1)
comes from interaction between absorbed CO* intermediates (inset in Figure 5c), which benefits C2+ production. The disappearance of both Raman signals at high current density indicates that these intermediates react at very fast CO2 reduction kinetics.49 However, Cu particles only show a single mode at ∼2070 cm−1, pointing to a less favorable C−C coupling on this electrode (Figure 5d and inset). Very interestingly, we observe that the Raman peaks from both electrodes experience a continuous negative shift as the applied current density increases, which can be explained by the electrochemical Stark effect, a phenomenon where the local electric field can regulate the interaction between the electrode and adsorbate, thus shifting the vibrational frequencies of intermediates.53,54
At lower wavenumbers (400−640 cm−1), our operando Raman spectroscopy measurements on a hierarchical Cu electrode reveal that peaks originated from surface CuOx disappeared immediately once negative currents were applied (Figure 5e), suggesting the reduction of surface oxide to metallic Cu. Meanwhile, several characteristic Raman peaks emerge, which arise from the Cu−CO (∼360 cm−1), CO2− (∼700, ∼1310, and ∼1550 cm−1), and CO32− (∼1070 cm−1) modes,49,55 respectively. The noticeable Cu−CO band at a large applied current density of 200 mA cm−2 indicates stable interaction between *CO and the Cu surface (Figure 5e), which supports the perspective that the hierarchical Cu electrode can stabilize the *CO intermediate and promote C−C coupling. After removing the current, the electrode surface was quickly reoxidized to Cu2O (Figure S45), consistent with our experimental observations above (Figures S31 and S32). Now we come to discuss the intrinsic factors that lead to the
marked efficiency and stability of our designed Cu electrode in catalyzing CO2RR to C2+ fuels at commercially relevant current densities (e.g., 300 mA cm−2). We outline two important scenarios for the performance enhancement. First, the hierarchical Cu architecture that mimics Setaria’s leaves induces remarkable water resistance and creates a robust CO2−electrolyte−Cu triple-phase boundary at the electrode, which allows for omnidirectional CO2 mass transfer, giving rise to a high local concentration of CO2 trapped near the active CO2RR surface. Moreover, the hydrophobicity of the electrode is rooted in its unique hierarchically sharp structure, which is highly stable to prevent flooding even at high-current operation. Nevertheless, the wettable Cu particulate electrode is readily flooded during CO2RR, and therefore the pathway of CO2 transfer is largely blocked, causing low CO2 concentration close to the catalyst for reaction. Second, we find clear evidence for the promoted C−C coupling on the hierarchical Cu electrode from our operando Raman spectroscopy tests. This is caused by the locally concentrated K+ ions at the highly structured electrode, which renders an alkali-metal-cation effect that not only stabilizes intermediates but also reduces the barrier of forming C−C bonds. As a consequence, we surmise that the new hierarchical electrode design allows for a robust gas−liquid−solid triple-phase boundary, sufficient CO2 mass transfer, and the favorable alkali-metal-cation effect, which together lead to advances in selectivity for C2+ production at large current densities, in stark contrast to the ordinary performance observed experimentally on the Cu particulate counterpart.

G
■ CONCLUSION In conclusion, the work reported here showcases that hierarchically structuring Cu needles on a GDL can lead to stable hydrophobicity of a CO2RR electrode without any hydrophobic coating. Besides preventing the GDL from being flooded, the obtained electrode can trap a gaseous layer near its surface, giving rise to a high local CO2 concentration that improves the CO2RR selectivity to C2+ products. Consequently, the electrode was very stable at a commercially relevant current density (here 300 mA cm−2) owing to the robust electrode−electrolyte interface guaranteed by the hydrophobicity. This bioinspired design thus suggests an electrode structuring route of creating a stable gas−liquid− solid triple-phase boundary that permits electrosynthesis of multicarbon fuels at industry-scale current densities.
■ EXPERIMENTAL SECTION Material Synthesis. All chemicals were used as received without further purification. The GDL (SGL 29BC) used in this work was purchased from Fuel Cell Store. The Cu dendrite catalyst was directly electrodeposited on the GDL. To improve the repeatability of the electrodeposition, the gas diffuse carbon paper was first treated by air plasma prior to catalyst deposition. The plating bath was a 0.1 M CuSO4·5H2O solution in deionized water (DIW) with pH = 2 adjusted by 2 M H2SO4. The Cu dendrite thin film was deposited under a constant potential of −0.7 V (vs Ag/AgCl) for 700 s in a three-electrode configuration where the Ag/AgCl electrode (saturated KCl) and Pt mesh were used as the reference electrode and counter electrode, respectively. The as-deposited film was rinsed with DIW and ethanol and then dried in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 4 h. The Cu particle catalyst was prepared by a hydrothermal method. In detail, 2 mmol of cupric(II) acetylacetonate (Cu(C5H7O2)2), 4 mL of propylamine (C3H7NH2), and 2 mL of 80% hydrazine hydrate (N2H4·H2O) were mixed in 30 mL of N,N-dimethylformamide (DMF). The above solution was put into a 50 mL Teflon-lined stainless steel autoclave and maintained at 200 °C for 8 h. Then the autoclave was cooled to room temperature naturally. The assynthesized Cu particle catalyst was rinsed with DIW and ethanol and then dried in a vacuum oven at 60 °C for 4 h. The Fouriertransform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy and baseline test were performed to ensure that no ethanol remained on the electrode before the CO2 electrolysis (Figure S17). Material Characterizations. Optical microscope images were obtained with a polarizing microscope (Leica DM2700P, Germany) equipped with a Leica MC190 HD camera. The morphology of the samples was determined by SEM (Zersss Supra 40) and TEM (JEOL 2010F(s)). HRTEM images were taken on a JEMARM 200F atomic resolution analytical microscope with an acceleration voltage of 200 kV. ICP-AES data were obtained by an Optima 7300 DV instrument. XRD was performed on a Japan Rigaku DMax-γA X-ray diffractometer with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.541 78 Å). XAS was carried out at the BL11U beamline of National Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory in Hefei, China. Water contact angles and CO2 bubble adhesion behaviors were analyzed via an OCA20 machine (DataPhysics, Germany) at room temperature. A water droplet with a ∼3 mm diameter was generated on a hydrophobic needle with a syringe driven by an infusion and withdrawal pump at 0.05 mL/min. Then water droplets were released to impact the surface of the electrodes. Simultaneously, the side-view images of the droplet were captured. For the measurements of CO2 bubble adhesion, the sample was clamped flat in a transparent quartz container and immersed in KHCO3 solution, and an individual CO2 bubble (about 2.0 μL) was injected from the syringe needle under solution to the electrode surface. In-situ Raman spectra were taken on a Raman microscope (Renishaw) with a 785 nm excitation laser. The CO2RR postreaction electrode was washed by deionized water and stored in a vacuum oven before measurements. Note that postreaction characterizations of
water contact angles and CO2 bubble adhesion behaviors of electrodes were performed after 10 h of CO2 electrolysis. Electrodes after CO2 electrolysis at a total current density of 300 mA cm
−2 for 10 min were also studied by SEM, XRD, and XPS.
Preparation of Cathode Electrodes. The as-deposited Cu dendrite gas-diffusion electrode (GDE) was directly used for electrochemical measurements. The Cu particle GDE was prepared by hand-painting the catalyst ink. In detail, 45 mg of catalyst powder was mixed with 2 mL of isopropanol containing 50 μL of Nafion ionomer solution (5 wt %), resulting in a homogeneous catalyst ink by ultrasonic dispersion. The resulting ink was uniformly spread on the GDL of 4 × 4 cm2 area by using an airbrush, yielding the Cu particle electrode with a catalyst loading of ∼2.8 mg cm−2, which was the same as that of the Cu dendrite electrode.
Electrochemical Measurements. All electrochemical measurements were performed in a flow cell with a VSP-300 potentiostat (Bio-Logic, France). For measurements in a flow cell, gaseous CO2 was passed through the gas chamber at the back side of the Cu GDE (1 × 1 cm2). The electrolyte (1 M KOH) was circulated through both the anode (nickel foam) and cathode chambers separated by the anion exchange membrane (AEM, Fumasep FAB-3-PK-130). The CO2 (99.999%) and KOH electrolyte flow was kept constant at 24 and 20 mL min−1 controlled by a mass flow controller (C100L, Sierra) and a peristaltic pump (BT100-2J, Longer Pump), respectively. The applied potentials were measured against a Ag/ AgCl reference electrode in saturated KCl and converted to the RHE reference scale with iR correction by
= + + × −E E iR(vs RHE) (vs Ag/AgCl) 0.205 (0.0591 pH) s (2)
where the solution resistance Rs was determined by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy at frequencies ranging from 0.1 Hz to 100 kHz.
CO2RR Product Analysis. To accurately quantify the gas products during CO2 electrolysis, the gas outlet flow rate from the reactor was carefully monitored by a mass flow meter (AST10-HLC, Asert Instruments) at each current density (Figure S15). The cathodic compartment was vented directly into the sampling loop of a gas chromatograph (GC-2014, Shimadzu). The GC analysis was set up to split the gas sample into two aliquots. One aliquot passed a thermal conductivity detector to quantify H2 concentration, and the other was routed through a flame ionization detector with a methanizer to quantitatively analyze the content of CO and alkane species. The faradaic efficiency for gas products was calculated by the following formula:

1H NMR spectra measured with water suppression using a presaturation method were collected on a Bruker 400 MHz spectrometer to test liquid products. Typically, 500 μL of electrolyte after CO2RR electrolysis was mixed with 100 μL of D2O containing 50 ppm (m/m) dimethyl sulfoxide as the internal standard. The same spectral acquisition parameters were used for all measurements to ensure complete relaxation and quantification. The presented data were the accumulated result of 32 scans.

Finite-Element-Method Simulations. In our work, the electrical double layer was modeled using the Gouy−Chapman−Stern model,
https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c01190 J. Am. Chem. Soc. XXXX, XXX, XXX−XXX
H
which consists of a Helmholtz layer and a diffusion layer. The former consists of a monolayer of surface-adsorbed hydrated K+ cation on the catalyst surface. The latter consisted of cations and anions, which is established as the result of a dynamic equilibrium between electrostatic forces and diffusion. In a steady state, the Poisson− Nerst−Planck equations could be solved to gain the electric field and K+ concentration near the catalyst surface. A two-dimensional model was built to represent the catalyst in this work. The diffusion coefficient D of the potassium ion was taken to be 2.14 × 10−9 m2 s−1 in water.46 The conductivity of the electrolyte (1 M KOH) and catalyst (metallic Cu) was taken to be 2.153 × 10−3 and 6.20 × 107 S m−1 (ref 56), respectively. In this model, the electric potential applied on the Cu catalyst was set to −1.0 V and the number of boundary layers on the catalyst surface was set to 8.
